hook: You know “My grace is sufficient for you”. But did you know Paul heard it after begging the Lord three times to take something away?
story:
The man who wrote this sentence had been stoned, shipwrecked three times, and let down a city wall in a basket to escape arrest. He also writes of a man he knew who was caught up into Paradise. And the sentence comes out of neither of those stories. It comes out of a prayer that was not answered the way he asked.

Paul knew Corinth from the inside. It was a Roman colony, a city that Julius Caesar refounded in 44 BC after Rome had burned it a century before. Paul stayed there “a year and six months”, and he later reminded the church how he had first arrived: “in weakness, in fear, and in much trembling”. Luke adds that the Lord spoke to him there in the night: “Don’t be afraid, but speak and don’t be silent”, and “I am with you”.

But by the time of this letter, other teachers had come to Corinth, and Paul calls them “the very best apostles”. He admits he is “unskilled in speech”. Pushed into comparing himself with them, he does something strange. He lists his sufferings: “in prisons more abundantly, in stripes above measure, and in deaths often”. Then he speaks, in the third person, of a man who was caught up into Paradise fourteen years before and heard things he may not repeat.

And then the turn. “By reason of the exceeding greatness of the revelations, that I should not be exalted excessively, a thorn in the flesh was given to me: a messenger of Satan to torment me”. He does not say what it was. He says what he did: “I begged the Lord three times that it might depart from me.”

The answer is our verse. The Lord does not take the thorn away in the words Paul records. He gives him this instead: “My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness.” And Paul, who had just spent chapters refusing to boast, says “Most gladly therefore I will rather glory in my weaknesses”.

moment:
Paul is writing to a church that has doubted him. Some in Corinth have been comparing him to rival teachers and finding him lacking. In reply he reluctantly boasts, and the boast turns upside down: what he points to is not his visions but his weakness. “For if I would desire to boast, I will not be foolish; for I will speak the truth.”

The thorn is the hinge. The text says it was “given to me”, that it came to keep him from being “exalted excessively”, and that he prayed about it three times. Then comes the answer, and the verse after it gives his conclusion: “Therefore I take pleasure in weaknesses, in injuries, in necessities, in persecutions, and in distresses, for Christ’s sake. For when I am weak, then am I strong.”

Notice what has and has not changed. The Lord’s answer is about grace and power. Paul’s own reading of it is that his weakness is where that power shows.
around: The same letter ends in the same key. Paul writes of Christ, “he was crucified through weakness, yet he lives through the power of God”, and then applies it to himself: “we also are weak in him”. The weakness he glories in is not a pose. It is the shape of the gospel he preached, a crucified Lord, and he says so from the first letter to Corinth onward.
after:
Paul’s weakness did not go away, and neither did his work. In the last chapter of this same letter he writes again of being weak in Christ and sharing his life. Years later, near the end, he writes to Timothy and reports the cost: “At my first defense, no one came to help me, but all left me.” In the same breath he reports what he found: “the Lord stood by me and strengthened me”. He also names a man who “did much evil” to him, “Alexander the coppersmith”, the very man Chrysostom later connected to the thorn, though the Bible itself never makes that link.

Then comes a sentence that reads like the end of a long road: “I have fought the good fight. I have finished the course. I have kept the faith.”

The verse itself kept traveling. In 1872 Spurgeon preached on it to his London congregation and told them to be content to keep their thorn if it kept them humble. Whatever you make of that advice, it shows how readers kept returning to Paul’s answer.
readings:
Nobody knows what the thorn was, and readers have guessed for nearly two thousand years. Some early writers thought of a bodily pain, such as a severe headache. Others, like Chrysostom, thought of people: Paul’s opponents, who made the work of preaching hard. Some have understood it as a struggle with temptation. Others have pointed to a physical illness, or to Paul’s grief over his own people’s refusal of the gospel. Several modern scholars conclude that the evidence does not allow a certain answer.

That silence may be part of the point. Because Paul never says what it was, readers across the centuries have been able to bring their own thorn to the verse.
argued:
In the late fourth century Chrysostom took up the question in a homily on this chapter. He knew the bodily view and set it aside: [[chrysostom]]

He read the thorn as hostile people, and read God’s reply as a gentle correction of a request that missed something: [[chrysostom-reply]]

Centuries later, in London, Spurgeon preached a whole sermon on the thorn and stressed one word in Paul’s sentence: it was given. He said of Paul: [[spurgeon]] Centuries apart, both men kept their eyes on what Paul received, not on what he lost.
point: The verse is not a promise that hard things will be taken away. In its own chapter, the Lord says no to the removal and yes to something else: grace that is enough, and power that shows in weakness. Paul’s answer to that is not resignation but gladness.
lesson:
If you have asked for something to be taken away, and it is still there, this verse does not ask you to pretend that is easy. Paul asked three times. Taking this verse seriously begins with taking that prayer seriously.

Then look at what the Lord gives him in its place. Not an explanation, but a word about grace that is enough and power that shows in weakness. And Paul does not claim that his weakness was good in itself. He says that the power of Christ rests on him there.

So it is fine to bring the real thing to God, again and again, and to say how much you want it gone. You can ask him what Paul’s answer might look like in your own life: where is grace already enough, even while the thorn stays? And if you do not share this faith, the verse still says something honest about people: strength is not the same as never being weak, and a person can carry a hard thing and still go on with gladness.

echoes.note: Isaiah says of God, “He gives power to the weak.” Paul’s reply from the Lord is the same truth said once more: power goes where weakness is.
In his first letter to the same city Paul writes, “God chose the weak things of the world that he might put to shame the things that are strong.” Our verse shows Paul living it.
Earlier in this letter Paul writes, “we have this treasure in clay vessels”, so that the power would be seen as God’s and not his own.
